## 1. Store Overview

My pretend Shopify store, **Atelier North**
([10b3ys-0m.myshopify.com](https://10b3ys-0m.myshopify.com)), is a curated
home goods brand selling kitchen, home & living, and bed & bath products. The
concept centers on "thoughtfully curated home essentials for modern living" —
positioning the store as a premium, design-forward alternative to big-box
home retailers. The target customer is a design-conscious adult shopper
furnishing or refreshing their home who values sourcing story and product
craftsmanship over low price. The assortment spans 9 SKUs across three
categories: Kitchen & Table (e.g., Hand-Carved Olive Wood Serving Board),
Home & Living (e.g., Stoneware Matcha Bowl), and Bed & Bath (e.g., Organic
Cotton Waffle Bath Towel Set).

## 3. Retail Technology Reflection

Building Atelier North taught me that Shopify functions as a full retail
operating system, not just a storefront builder. Setting up products,
collections, navigation, and policies made clear how much of the "retail"
work — merchandising rules, inventory status, checkout logic — is handled
declaratively through the platform rather than through custom code. I also
learned that Shopify's default behaviors (like inventory-driven "Sold out"
states) directly shape the customer experience, and that platform
configuration choices are retail decisions, not just technical ones. Testing
the customer journey end to end showed me how tightly the platform couples
storefront presentation with backend inventory and cart logic, and how a
single misconfiguration (like the sold-out/cart mismatch I found in
Assignment 8) can break the entire funnel even when every individual page
looks polished.

## 4. Merchandising Reflection

Working through product catalog setup, collections, and navigation taught me
that merchandising on Shopify is really an exercise in information
architecture. Deciding which three categories to expose in the nav, how to
group products into collections, and how to write product copy that sells a
narrative rather than just specs all directly affected how easy the store
was to browse. I learned that collection filtering (by availability and
price) is a merchandising tool as much as a technical feature — it lets a
shopper self-select into the products relevant to them. I also learned that
storefront design and merchandising can't be evaluated separately from
inventory accuracy: a beautifully merchandised collection page still fails
the customer if every item is unavailable, which was the central issue I
uncovered in my customer journey testing.

## 5. Analytics Reflection

Reviewing the built-in Shopify Analytics dashboard showed me what a
retailer sees by default — gross sales, returning customer rate, orders
fulfilled — and how those metrics stay at zero without real traffic and
transactions. This made concrete why GA4 integration matters: GA4 is what
would let me see behavior *before* a purchase decision (sessions, page
views, funnel drop-off by stage) rather than just post-purchase totals.
Connecting this to the CPP Farm Store dashboard project, where I was
responsible for designing dashboard sections to evaluate omnichannel and
ecommerce campaign performance, reinforced that analytics only becomes
useful once it's organized around specific business questions (channel
performance, campaign ROI, customer behavior) rather than just displayed as
raw metrics. Testing my own store's customer journey was a useful complement
to that dashboard work — it showed me firsthand what a broken step in the
funnel (like the sold-out inconsistency) looks like from the customer side,
which is exactly the kind of drop-off a GA4 funnel report would need to
surface.

## 6. CPP Farm Store Application

1. **Funnel and drop-off visibility.** The customer journey testing method I
   used on Atelier North — walking homepage → collection → product → cart →
   checkout and logging where the experience breaks — is directly
   transferable to CPP Farm Store. A GA4 funnel exploration could quantify
   where real customers abandon the path, the same way I manually caught the
   sold-out/cart mismatch on my own store.
2. **Inventory and merchandising accuracy as a conversion lever.** My
   experience with sold-out statuses blocking checkout shows CPP Farm Store
   that inventory data quality is itself a conversion driver — a GA4/Shopify
   dashboard should flag high-traffic products that are unavailable, since
   these are lost-sale opportunities.
3. **Channel-level dashboard design.** The dashboard sections I designed for
   the CPP Farm Store GP6 project (evaluating omnichannel and ecommerce
   campaign performance) apply the same principle I practiced on Atelier
   North's Shopify Analytics page: organize metrics (sessions, conversion
   rate, average order value) by the questions the business actually needs
   answered — in CPP Farm Store's case, comparing in-store/omnichannel
   performance against pure ecommerce channel performance.

## 7. Final Self-Assessment

I'm proud of the visual and content consistency across Atelier North — the
color palette, typography, and benefit-driven product copy give the store a
cohesive, premium feel from the homepage through individual product pages.
With more time, I would fix the inventory configuration so every product
supports a full end-to-end checkout test, and I would generate real test
traffic so the Shopify Analytics and GA4 dashboards showed actual session,
conversion, and sales-by-product data instead of a zero-state — that would
let me evaluate real customer behavior rather than just the static storefront
design.
